name: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension

ethnicAssociations: Higher incidence in obese women of reproductive age
May be more common in Black women

criteria.description: Normal neurological examination except for cranial nerve abnormalities (typically CN VI palsy)
Normal brain parenchyma on MRI (with and without gadolinium, including MRV)
Elevated lumbar puncture opening pressure (>25 cmH2O in adults, >28 cmH2O in children)
MRI signs: empty sella, optic nerve sheath distension, flattened posterior globe, transverse venous sinus stenosis

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Papilledema, normal neurological exam (except CN VI), normal brain imaging, elevated opening pressure, and normal CSF composition. IIH without papilledema (IIHWOP) is possible but requires additional criteria.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Must exclude secondary causes of raised intracranial pressure: venous sinus thrombosis, medications (tetracyclines, vitamin A, growth hormone), and systemic diseases.

laboratory: Elevated CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture (>25 cmH2O in adults)
Normal CSF cell count, protein, and glucose
Metabolic screening to exclude secondary causes
imaging: MRI: distension of perioptic subarachnoid space
MRV: bilateral transverse sinus stenosis (common but may be secondary to raised pressure)
Normal brain parenchyma (no mass, hydrocephalus, or venous thrombosis)
other: Formal perimetry (Humphrey visual fields) showing enlarged blind spots and peripheral field constriction
OCT showing peripapillary RNFL thickening (acute) or thinning (chronic atrophy)
Fundus photography for papilledema grading (Frisen scale)

distinguishingFeatures: Chiari has tonsillar herniation on MRI
Chiari headache is occipital and Valsalva-induced
Chiari does not have elevated CSF pressure
CVST shows venous filling defect on MRV/CTV
CVST has identifiable prothrombotic risk factors
NPH presents with gait, cognitive, and urinary triad
NPH has normal or low opening pressure

redFlags: Fulminant IIH with rapid vision loss requires urgent surgical intervention (optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunting)
Progressive visual field loss despite maximal medical therapy indicates treatment failure
Atypical demographics (male, thin, elderly) should prompt aggressive search for secondary causes
CSF abnormalities (pleocytosis, elevated protein) exclude IIH and suggest alternative diagnosis
Medication review essential: tetracyclines, vitamin A/retinoids, growth hormone can cause secondary intracranial hypertension
IIH without papilledema is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring extensive workup
references: Friedman DI, et al. Revised diagnostic criteria for the pseudotumor cerebri syndrome in adults and children. Neurology. 2013;81(13):1159-1165.
Mollan SP, et al. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: consensus guidelines on management. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 2018;89(10):1088-1100.
Markey KA, et al. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: the evolving landscape. Nat Rev Neurol. 2024.
